newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: INTERVIEW-Cyrix sees big gains in Asia.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Cyrix sees big gains in Asia.

text.p: U.S.-based chip maker Cyrix Corp, a rival to Intel, expects the Asian market to contribute a sharply higher share of its global revenue this year, a company official said on Monday.

K.B. Lim, Cyrix's country manager for South Asia Pacific, said it was positioned to capture the vast and price-conscious Asian market and its revenue contribution was expected to climb to 35 percent from 22 percent by the end of 1997.
"Cyrix is in the right place and at the right time ...in this region (Asia) to capture the strong growth in the market," Lim told Reuters in an interview.
"Asia now has 22 percent of corporate revenue but because the market is booming, we are trying to grow to as high as 35 percent," he said.
Lim said growth in the region was strong in the first quarter and he expected the trend to pick up with the 35 percent contribution target possibly hit by the end of 1997.
Cyrix recorded a revenue of US$183.8 million in 1996 but was in the red with a loss of US$25.9 million.
In the first quarter this year, it beat Wall Street's expectations with a net profit of US$6.61 million on revenue of US$75.6 million.
On Friday Cyrix fired another salvo at Intel with the launch of its 6x86MX chip that will compete with Intel's Pentium II at half the price. It was launched in Singapore on Monday.
The fastest version has speed of up to 233 megahertz and a 266 megahertz version is expected in the fourth quarter.
Lim expected worldwide shipments of the 6x86MX to hit five million units in the first year, about the same amount as the 6x86 processor in its initial year.
Volume production would start from the third quarter.

The 6x86MX launch was ahead of schedule and was also timely after Intel's recent warning that its second-quarter results would be below expectations, partly because it could not make enough Pentium IIs and Pentiums with MMX, Lim said.
The Cyrix strategy was to offer top performance at lower prices, targetting at entry-level and midrange multimedia personal computers priced in the US$1,500 range, he said.
The company was benefitting from the wave of information technology consciousness in Asia -- in education, in the homes and at the government level, he added.
The company was looking for local partners to work on government projects in countries like Singapore.
In Asia, it works through local distributors and dealers and ensured there was one to two weeks of inventories in each country to meet demand, Lim said.
As the new kid on the block, Cyrix would be participating in more tradeshows and promotional campaigns to create awareness of its products.
Lim said Cyrix was monitoring Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) which has a similar strategy with its lower-priced K6 and K5 chips that match Intel's top performing Pentium Pro processors.
But there was room for more players in the market, he said.
"It is no joke when you are competing as a lone soldier against Intel," Lim said. New players were more likely to eat into Intel's share rather than Cyrix's, he added.
--Singapore newsroom (65-8703080)
